studies.title: Everything Already Says It
studies.meaning: The surah opens with a completed action: glorification has been performed by everything in the heavens and the earth. The verb is in the past tense, which the commentators note as a claim that this is settled rather than ongoing or aspirational. Nothing is asked of the reader. Two names close the ayah, one for irresistible power and one for wisdom, and the pairing matters for what follows, since the surah is about to describe a defeat and insist it was neither accident nor cruelty.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, opening a surah that will deal with the expulsion of a tribe from Medina in the years after the migration. The community was in a period of sharp insecurity, with agreements inside the town breaking down. The opening ayah says nothing about any of that. The commentators read it as the frame: the surah places the whole episode inside a universe already engaged in praise before it names a single party.

keyTerms.note: From a root for swimming or moving smoothly through water. The word carries motion, and its religious sense is declaring God free of any defect, so the praise is subtractive rather than decorative.
From a root meaning to be rare, precious and hard to reach. It joins scarcity and strength, so the name says both that nothing overpowers Him and that nothing is comparable to Him.
From a root for a bridle that restrains an animal, which also gives the words for judgement and for governing. Wisdom in this vocabulary is the placing of limits, not the accumulation of knowledge.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian religious language already had words for praising: poets praised patrons, and pilgrims called out formulas approaching the sanctuary. What was unusual was assigning the act to things that do not speak. Stones, wells, herds and the ridge line above a valley were part of a landscape people read for signs rather than for worship. The opening puts all of it into a single sentence with one verb.
studies.didYouKnow: Five surahs of the Quran open with this verb of glorification: 57, 59, 61, 62 and 64. Three of them, including this one, use the completed past form, and the other two use the ongoing present. The five sit close together in the order of the Book and are known collectively by that opening word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Praise is described as a fact about the world rather than a duty laid on it, which shifts what a human act of worship is: joining something already underway, not starting it. The past tense removes any suggestion that the universe waits for people to begin. And placing power beside wisdom at the outset commits the surah in advance, since everything it will report about a defeat must be read as both irresistible and considered.

crossReferences.why: Says the seven heavens and all in them glorify Him, and that people do not grasp how.
Describes birds in flight, each one knowing its own prayer and its manner of praise.
Opens another surah with the identical wording, and goes on to a different subject entirely.

studies.applyIt: Pick something in view from where you are sitting that has no say in the matter: a tree, a wall, the sky through a window. Look at it for thirty seconds with this ayah in mind. The claim is that it is already doing what you are trying to remember to do. Nothing is asked of you here except noticing.

studies.title: The Fortresses Did Not Hold
studies.meaning: The ayah reports an expulsion and then dismantles two expectations at once. The believers did not think it would happen; the other party thought their strongholds would hold. Both assumptions are named and both are set aside by a single clause about God arriving from an unreckoned direction. The strangest detail is the demolition: houses pulled apart by their own occupants as well as by the besiegers. It closes by telling people with eyes to draw the lesson.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators agree that this describes the expulsion of one of the Jewish tribes of Medina after an agreement between them and the community broke down, and that the siege ended without a general battle. The tribe departed northward and elsewhere. Reports differ on the details of the negotiation and the terms of departure, and the Quran gives none of them, keeping the account at the level of what happened and why.

keyTerms.note: The word the surah is named after. It means driving people together and out, and is used elsewhere of the gathering at the resurrection, which gives the historical event an echo it would not otherwise carry.

From a root for being inaccessible and fortified, which also gives the word for a chaste person and for a well-guarded thing. The image is of something sealed, and the ayah reports the seal failing from an unexpected side.
A word for fear that fills and hollows out, distinct from ordinary fright. It appears four times in the Quran, always of something placed into hearts rather than caused by what an enemy did.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The settlements around Medina were built around stone towers, some of them several storeys high, with a single door and a store of water and dates inside. A family could hold one for weeks. They were the whole security architecture of an oasis, and the reason a small group could refuse a much larger one. Dismantling a house meant prising out its timber and door frames, which were worth more than the walls.
studies.didYouKnow: The word this surah takes its name from occurs in it exactly once, in this ayah, where it is called the first gathering. The word for terror appears four times in the whole Quran, and in every case it is described as being cast into hearts by God rather than produced by an enemy's strength.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah insists on a cause the participants could not see, and it does so without denying what they did see. Fortresses were real, the siege was real, the hands that pulled the timber out were human hands. What is added is a direction, arriving from where nobody reckoned. That phrasing protects the account from becoming a claim about superior tactics or numbers, and the closing instruction asks for interpretation rather than triumph.

crossReferences.why: Describes another episode in Medina with the same phrase about terror cast into hearts.
Uses the same expression for terror at a different engagement, again attributing it to God rather than to force.
States that God grants and strips sovereignty, which is the general principle this episode illustrates.

studies.applyIt: Think of a protection you have arranged for yourself: savings, a qualification, a person who would take your call. There is nothing wrong with any of it. Just name, once, the thing it would not cover. This ayah is not against walls. It is against the quiet assumption that you have already thought of everything.

studies.title: Exile Instead Of Destruction
studies.meaning: A counterfactual is stated and left in place: if departure had not been decreed for them, something worse would have followed in this life. The passage therefore describes what happened as the lighter of two written outcomes, without calling it mercy. The second ayah supplies the ground, and the verb it uses for their opposition means to place oneself on the far side of something. The general clause that follows widens the case beyond the people involved.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, continuing the account of the expulsion. The tribe left Medina under terms that allowed them to carry away what their camels could bear, which the commentators contrast with the outcome the passage says was avoided. The setting is a town where several agreements between groups had failed in succession, and where the Quran is explaining an outcome to a community that had expected either a battle or nothing.

keyTerms.note: A specific word for leaving a place and abandoning it, used of a whole population rather than an individual. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it names the event without describing it as flight or as defeat.

From the word for a side or a split, so the verb means putting oneself in the opposite half of something. The image is of a break running through what was one thing, which is what a broken agreement is.
From a root for a heel and for what follows behind. The word treats a consequence as something that comes after and catches up, which keeps the sense of sequence rather than of arbitrary infliction.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Exile was among the heaviest sentences a tribal society could impose, heavier in some ways than a fine or a killing. A group that left its palm groves lost the only capital it had, since date gardens took a decade to establish and could not be carried. Wells, terraces and grafted trees stayed behind. Departure meant beginning again somewhere with animals, cloth and whatever could be loaded.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for the departure of a whole population occurs only once in the Quran, in this ayah. Arabic had a large vocabulary for the movement of groups, and the choice of this particular term places the event in the register of an evacuation ordered from above rather than of a rout or an escape.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are held together that people usually separate. The passage says a hard outcome was the milder of the possibilities, and it says so without asking anyone to feel grateful about it. That is a particular kind of honesty: the lightening is stated as a fact of the record, not offered as consolation. And by giving a reason, the passage refuses to leave the event unexplained, which is what would make it arbitrary.

crossReferences.why: States that punishment was withheld while certain conditions held, the same logic of a worse outcome averted.
Continues the account, describing the divisions inside the group whose opposition this passage names.
Uses the same verb for making a breach with the messenger after guidance has become clear.

studies.applyIt: Think of a bad outcome from your own life that you know could have been worse, and let yourself say both halves of that sentence out loud. Most of us can manage one half or the other. Holding the two together is uncomfortable and accurate, which is exactly how this passage handles the event it is reporting.

studies.title: The Palms And The Permission
studies.meaning: A dispute about conduct during the siege is settled in one sentence. Whichever was done, felling the trees or leaving them standing on their roots, both are placed under God's leave. The ayah does not rank the two options or praise either party. It then gives a purpose clause that attaches to the whole episode rather than to the trees. Commentators read the ayah as closing an argument among the besiegers about whether the felling had been wrong.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The commentators report with broad agreement that some date palms were cut during the siege and that this caused an objection, since destroying productive trees ran against everything the region's economy assumed. The ayah answers that objection. Reports differ on how many trees and on who raised the complaint, and the Quran names neither, which is consistent with how the whole surah handles the episode.

keyTerms.note: A word for a variety of date palm, occurring only here in the Quran. Commentators differ over which variety, and the specificity matters: the ayah is about actual named trees, not about vegetation in general.
The plural of a word meaning a base or origin, used in Arabic for the foundations of an argument as well as the root of a plant. Leaving a tree on its roots is leaving it able to bear again.
From a root meaning to listen and then to permit. Permission in this vocabulary begins with hearing, so the word carries a sense of something granted attentively rather than allowed by default.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A date palm took seven or eight years to bear and far longer to reach full yield, and a family's standing was counted in trees. Groves were inherited, named and quarrelled over. Cutting one was close to unthinkable outside a siege, and even raiders generally left them, because next season's dates fed everyone eventually. The objection the ayah answers was not sentimental; it was about destroying something nobody could quickly replace.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the palm tree in this ayah appears nowhere else in the Quran. It is one of a small number of words that occur a single time in the whole text, and its meaning was already debated in the earliest commentaries, which record several proposals for which variety of date palm is meant.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah takes a question about conduct and answers it by relocating the agency, which is a move worth noticing. It does not say the felling was good or that it was necessary. It says the outcome, either way, fell inside what was allowed, and it attaches the purpose to the disgrace of those who had broken faith rather than to the trees. That keeps a specific act from becoming a general principle about destruction.

crossReferences.why: Reports the same siege, including houses pulled down by their own occupants, which this ayah's question follows from.
Describes the ruin of crops and livestock by someone who gains power as corruption God does not like.
Names date palms among the things God produces, which is why cutting one needed answering at all.

studies.applyIt: Think of an argument you are still having with yourself about a decision that is already made and cannot be reversed. Write the two options side by side, honestly, and then stop. This ayah ends a dispute by declining to rank the alternatives. Some questions are worth settling; this kind is worth setting down.

studies.title: No Horse Was Spurred
studies.meaning: The property is described by how it did not arrive. No cavalry charge, no camel forced across country, nothing the community can claim as effort. A specific word is used for wealth that comes back without fighting, and the point of the ayah is to detach it from the category of battle spoils. What replaces the claim of effort is a statement about God giving authority to messengers, which places the outcome outside the ledger of who earned what.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The tribe's land and property in Medina came into the community's hands without a general engagement, since the siege ended in departure. That created a genuine question: property taken in battle was distributed by a known rule, and this was not that. The commentators treat this ayah and the next as establishing the distinct category, and they read the denial of horses and camels as answering an expectation the fighters already had.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a shadow turning back in the afternoon and for anything returning to where it belongs. The word treats the property as reverting rather than as being seized, which is the whole argument of the ayah.
A verb for driving an animal hard, occurring only here in the Quran. It names the physical effort of a raid precisely, which is what makes its denial specific rather than general.
A collective noun for camels used as mounts, distinct from the words for camels as property or as herds. It appears once in the Quran, and pairing it with horses covers both kinds of expedition.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A raid was expensive before it was profitable. Horses were rare and costly in Arabia and were fed grain rather than left to graze, so a man who kept one had invested heavily. Camels wore down on hard marches and needed weeks to recover. Anyone who had spurred an animal towards a settlement had a claim afterwards that everyone recognised, and the size of the claim tracked what the effort had cost him.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of this ayah's words appear nowhere else in the Quran: the verb for driving an animal to a gallop, and the collective noun for riding camels. Both belong to the technical vocabulary of a raid, and the ayah reaches for them only in order to deny that either one applied here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Entitlement is the question, and the ayah answers it by examining causes rather than by asserting authority. Because no one exerted himself, no one holds a claim by exertion, which is a piece of reasoning anyone in that society could follow. The theological claim rides on the practical one: what arrives without effort has to be attributed somewhere, and the ayah attributes it, then hands the distribution to the passage that follows.

crossReferences.why: Takes up the distribution of exactly this property in the next ayah, naming who it reaches.
Sets out the rule for property taken in an actual engagement, the category this ayah is distinguishing itself from.
Speaks of land and homes inherited including ground never stepped on, the same idea of an unearned transfer.

studies.applyIt: Take one good thing in your life and try, seriously, to trace the part of it you did not arrange: who introduced you, what happened to be open that week, the health that held. Write down two items. This ayah begins by subtracting effort from an outcome, and the subtraction is what makes room for gratitude.

studies.title: So It Does Not Circulate
studies.meaning: A list of recipients is given and then a purpose clause explains the list. The named categories run from the messenger's relatives down to the traveller with nothing, and the reason offered is economic: so that the property does not stay in rotation among the wealthy. The word for that rotation appears only here. The ayah then widens sharply, instructing that what the messenger gives be taken and what he withholds be left, which commentators read as extending well past this distribution.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan. The property left behind by the departing tribe was substantial, chiefly land and date groves inside the oasis, and it arrived without an engagement that would have triggered the ordinary rule for spoils. The commentators describe genuine expectation among the fighters. These ayat settle the matter by naming categories rather than individuals, and by stating a reason nobody could dispute on its own terms.

keyTerms.note: From a root for turning and taking turns, which also gives the word for a state or dynasty. It names wealth that circulates within a closed set of hands, and it occurs only here in the Quran.
The Arabic idiom for a traveller, literally the child of the way, since the road is what he belongs to while he is on it. It names someone with resources at home and none where he stands.
From a root for reaching an end or a boundary. The command is to arrive at a stopping point rather than to resist an urge, which makes it a word about limits rather than about struggle.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In an oasis economy, land was the only asset that produced year after year, and it tended to consolidate. A poor family sold a corner of a grove in a bad season, and a wealthy one bought it; over two generations, ownership narrowed. Everyone could name the handful of households that had been buying. A rule directing a large windfall away from exactly those households was not abstract to anyone hearing it.
studies.didYouKnow: The word translated as circulating among the wealthy occurs only once in the Quran, in this ayah. Its root later supplied the ordinary Arabic word for a state, so the term that names wealth going round a closed circle of hands is the same one that came to name political power itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A reason is given for a distribution, which is not the usual shape of a command. The stated aim is the circulation of wealth through a whole society rather than the reward of any group, and that aim is placed in the text itself rather than left to be inferred. The instruction about taking and leaving then generalises the messenger's authority, which the commentators have long read as extending past the case in hand.

crossReferences.why: Names a comparable set of recipients for property taken in an engagement, sharing the orphan, the poor and the traveller.
Lists the categories for alms, overlapping with these and adding others, so the vocabulary of need is shared.
Explains why this property fell outside the ordinary rule, since no expedition was mounted for it.

studies.applyIt: Look at where your regular giving goes and ask whether it reaches anyone outside the circle you already move in. Most giving follows relationships, which is natural and not a fault. This ayah is interested in the shape of the whole flow. Add one recipient this month who has no way of thanking you.

studies.title: Driven Out And Still Seeking
studies.meaning: The recipients are named by what happened to them and by what they wanted. They were driven from homes and property, and the ayah puts those two losses in one phrase, so the material and the domestic go together. Then their motive is stated in the present tense: seeking favour and approval, and coming to the aid of God and His messenger. The closing verdict uses a word for truthfulness, applied to people rather than to statements.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, specifying the first category among those the previous ayah named. The emigrants had left Mecca with nothing and had been in Medina for some years, many still dependent on host families. The commentators describe this distribution as the moment their long dependence eased. The ayah's description of them is unusually warm for a passage about property, which the commentators note as deliberate rather than incidental.

keyTerms.note: An active participle from a root for cutting ties and departing, not merely for travelling. The word makes the leaving the person's own act, which matters beside the passive verb the same ayah uses for being driven out.

An intensive form for settled acceptance, used in the Quran almost entirely of God's satisfaction with people. Placing it beside the word for material favour makes the pair cover both what they lost and what they were after.
From the root for truth, but applied to persons rather than to speech, so it names people whose conduct matches their claim. The same root gives the ordinary Arabic word for a charitable gift.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man who left Mecca left a trade, a house and a network of relatives who guaranteed his debts. In Medina he arrived as a guest, and guests in Arabia were honoured and also, inevitably, dependent. Several emigrants took up unfamiliar work, carrying water or trading in a market whose customs were not theirs. Years of that wears on a person in a society where standing came from what a family held.
studies.didYouKnow: The definite plural naming the emigrants appears in five ayat of the Quran. One of them, 9:100, sets out the same three-tier picture this passage builds across three consecutive ayat: those who emigrated, those who received them, and those who came afterwards. The two passages describe one community from different angles.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Need and merit are named in the same breath and neither is allowed to cancel the other. The ayah could have justified the distribution on need alone, which would have been sufficient, or on service alone, which would have been flattering. It gives both, and then adds a verdict about character. That combination refuses to treat the poor as objects of a transfer; the recipients are described as people with a record, not a condition.

crossReferences.why: Sets out the same three groups, emigrants, supporters and those who followed, with God pleased with all of them.
Names those who believed and migrated as looking forward to God's mercy, in the same vocabulary.
Describes the group that received them, and is the second panel of the picture this ayah begins.

studies.applyIt: If you have ever had to accept help for a long stretch, you know the hard part is not the lack but the position. Think of someone currently in that position near you, and find a way this week to give them something to do rather than something to take. This ayah describes its recipients by what they were doing, not only by what they lacked.

studies.title: Preferring Others While Short
studies.meaning: The people described are named by where they were rather than by what they did: they had settled the home and the faith before the arrivals came. Three things follow. They love the newcomers, they feel no want in their chests for what the newcomers were given, and they prefer others over themselves while short themselves. The closing clause moves the difficulty inward: what has to be escaped is not poverty but the grasping of one's own soul.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, after the expulsion of a Medinan tribe and the distribution of what was left behind. The ayat just before assign that property largely to the emigrants from Mecca, who had arrived with nothing, rather than to the people of Medina who had hosted them for years. This ayah describes how the hosts received that decision, and the classical sources treat it as praise of a specific group at a specific moment.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking a place as a dwelling. It governs two objects here, the home and the faith, so the grammar puts belief and residence in the same category: something you move into and live in.
From a root meaning to choose and to leave a trace. The word became the classical name for giving away what you need yourself, and it is distinguished from generosity with a surplus.
A stronger word than ordinary meanness, combining the desire to keep with the desire to acquire. Attaching it to the soul makes it a condition to be rescued from rather than a habit to be corrected.
The word names a chink or opening, the gaps in a wall, and by extension a hole in a person's own provision. It pictures poverty as something you can see through rather than as a quantity.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: When the Meccans arrived in Medina they had no houses, no land and no trade contacts. The people of Medina paired off with them, sharing homes, splitting date palms and finding them work. The arrangement lasted for years and cost the hosts real income in a town where cultivable land was scarce and irrigation expensive. This ayah was heard by people still living inside that arrangement.
studies.didYouKnow: The closing clause of this ayah appears a second time in the Quran, word for word, in a later surah, where it follows an instruction to spend rather than a portrait of a community. The repetition detaches it from this occasion: what is described here as the achievement of one group in one year is stated elsewhere as a general condition of success.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah locates the obstacle precisely. Not wealth, not poverty, and not the other person: the thing standing between a human being and success is named as the grasping quality of his own soul, and the verb used for escaping it is passive. You are protected from it rather than defeating it. That makes generosity, in this description, less an achievement than a rescue, which is why the passage reads as praise without any trace of flattery.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the clause about being saved from one's own grasping, attaching it to spending rather than to a community.
Extends the portrait to later generations, whose share is to ask forgiveness and to carry no resentment.
Shows the same preference in a single act, food given away by people who wanted it themselves.

studies.applyIt: Give something away this week that you would actually like to keep. Not money you will not miss. A ticket, an afternoon, the last of something. Then notice the small internal argument that starts up while you do it. That argument is what the ayah names, and being able to hear it is most of the work.

studies.title: The Ones Who Came After
studies.meaning: The third group in the sequence is defined by a prayer rather than by a deed. They ask forgiveness for themselves and for those who preceded them in faith, and then ask for something more specific: that no rancour towards believers be placed in their hearts. Commentators note that the request is about the inside of a person, and that it is phrased as something God does or refrains from doing. The prayer closes on two names of tenderness.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, completing a sequence that began with the emigrants and continued with those who received them. The commentators read this third group as everyone who would come later, which is unusual: a passage about distributing property in one town extends itself to people not yet born. The Medina of the time already had frictions between the two earlier groups, and the prayer names exactly the feeling that frictions leave behind.

keyTerms.note: From the root for a race and for arriving first. It occurs only here in the Quran, and it casts earlier believers as runners already down the track rather than as a generation to be judged.
From a root for something entering and lodging inside, also used of a shackle. It names resentment that has settled in and become part of the fittings rather than a passing anger.

The strongest word in Arabic for pity that acts, held in the classical accounts to be more intense than the ordinary term for mercy. It is paired with mercy in nine ayat of the Quran, and this is one of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Medina in these years was two communities learning to be one. The households that had taken in emigrants had given up rooms, shares of land and standing, and the emigrants had spent years as guests. Both arrangements strain. Arab society had elaborate customs for hospitality precisely because everyone knew how quickly generosity curdles when it lasts. A prayer about grudges was not abstract in a town built on those arrangements.
studies.didYouKnow: The noun for a lodged grudge appears three times in the Quran. The other two, at 7:43 and 15:47, both describe it being pulled out of the chests of the people of the Garden. This ayah is the only place the word occurs inside a prayer, asking for that removal now rather than later.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer treats an inner state as something to petition for rather than to manufacture. That is a considered position: resentment is notoriously hard to argue oneself out of, and the request acknowledges as much by addressing it upward. Including earlier believers in the plea for forgiveness also builds a relationship in one direction only, since the people prayed for cannot answer, which removes any question of exchange.

crossReferences.why: Describes the same rancour being drawn out of the chests of those admitted to the Garden.
Describes the group this prayer names as those who preceded, and their freedom from grudging.
Recalls hearts reconciled after enmity, which is the gift this prayer asks be kept in place.

studies.applyIt: Say this prayer once for someone you have quietly written off, by name, without telling them and without expecting the feeling to change today. Grudges do not respond to argument, which is why the ayah puts the request where it does. Notice what it costs you to say the name at all.

studies.title: Three Promises, All Emphatic
studies.meaning: A promise is quoted in full, and its grammar is the point. Two of its three clauses carry the strongest emphatic markers Arabic has, and the third is closed with a word meaning ever. We will leave with you, we will never obey anyone against you, we will support you. Nothing is hedged. The ayah then ends with one short clause of testimony that cancels all three at once, and commentators read that contrast in length as deliberate.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, during or just before the siege. The commentators report that messages were sent from inside Medina to the tribe under pressure, urging them to hold out and promising support that never came. Reports differ on the wording and on who carried them, and the Quran gives the promise rather than the names. The general situation is agreed: assurances circulating in a town where nobody could be sure who would act.

keyTerms.note: From the word for a jerboa's burrow with a second exit, dug so the animal can bolt when the first hole is blocked. The image is of a prepared escape rather than of simple dishonesty.

Carries a prefixed particle and a doubled ending, the double emphasis Arabic reserves for oaths. Quoting the promise in this form is what makes the closing verdict land, since nothing weaker was said.

The verb for giving testimony in a dispute. Using it here puts God in the position of a witness rather than a judge, which is the position that settles a matter where two accounts contradict each other.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Promises of support were the currency of Arabian politics. A tribe under threat sent riders out to allies and counted the answers, because the count decided whether to fight or to negotiate. An assurance given and not kept was among the worst things said about a man in poetry, worse than cowardice, because a whole group had staked its decision on it. Everyone knew someone who had been left waiting.
studies.didYouKnow: The Arabic word for playing a double part comes from the name of a burrow with a hidden second exit, which the jerboa digs so it can break out the far side when a predator blocks the entrance. The term was already in use for the animal's tunnel before the Quran applied it to a way of living.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats a promise as evidence about the promiser rather than as a fact about the future. That is why the verdict can be delivered before anything happens: the ayah is not predicting, it is reading. Placing God as witness rather than as judge is precise, because the question at issue is what is true now, inside people, and testimony is the instrument for exactly that kind of question.

crossReferences.why: Unwinds the promise clause by clause in the next ayah, in the same order it was given.
Uses the same structure of a declaration quoted and then answered by God's own testimony.
Reports people saying with their mouths what is not in their hearts, in the same kind of moment.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next promise you are about to make with an intensifier attached: definitely, absolutely, no matter what. Take the intensifier off and see whether you still want to say the sentence. If you do, it was a real promise. If the sentence weakens without it, that is worth knowing before anyone is relying on you.

studies.title: Taken Apart Clause By Clause
studies.meaning: The promise of the previous ayah is dismantled in the order it was made. They will not leave; they will not help; and if they somehow do help, they will turn their backs. Then a fourth clause is added that was not in the promise at all, saying they themselves will not be helped. The passage does not argue or produce evidence. It simply runs the same sentence again with each verb negated.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, and events bore it out: the promised support did not arrive and the besieged tribe left. The commentators use that outcome to explain why the passage is stated so flatly, as a description of something already known rather than a warning. The setting is a town in which several groups were calculating which way to move, and in which a stated intention and an actual decision were routinely different things.

keyTerms.note: Carries the same doubled emphatic ending the promise used, now attached to the opposite action. The grammar of the assurance is turned around and pointed back at the people who spoke it.
The plural of the word for a back or a rear, used in the Quran only of flight from an engagement. Turning the backs is the technical phrase for a rout, not a general image of retreat.

A passive of the verb used three times already across these two ayat for giving support. The switch to the passive at the end puts the promisers in the position they had offered to fill for someone else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Turning the back was the moment a battle ended in Arabian warfare. Lines held while men faced each other, and a rout began when a few at the edge broke and ran, since a fleeing man exposed the flank of everyone beside him. Poets who praised a warrior praised him for holding. The phrase in this ayah is not a metaphor; it names the exact instant everything came apart.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for turning the backs occurs three times in the Quran, at 33:15, 48:22 and here, and in each case it describes flight from an engagement rather than ordinary retreat. The verb for giving support appears four times across this ayah and the one before it, ending in the passive with nobody left to supply it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says what people will do before they do it, which raises the question of whether they were free to do otherwise. The classical reading does not treat this as compulsion but as knowledge: the description follows from what these people already are, in the same way that anyone who knows a friend well can say in advance how a hard conversation will go. What is settled is the character, not the choice.

crossReferences.why: Gives the promise this ayah takes apart, in the same order and with the same verbs.
Recalls a covenant made not to turn the backs, and notes that such covenants are asked about.
Describes people concealing within themselves what they would not say aloud after a setback.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you have been meaning to do for someone, and estimate honestly how likely you are to do it this week. Not how much you want to. How likely. If the number is low, either put it in the calendar today or tell the person plainly. This ayah is unkind about the third option.

studies.title: The Fear That Ranks Higher
studies.meaning: One comparison carries the ayah. The dread these people feel towards other human beings is greater than what they feel towards God, and the ayah states it as a measurement rather than as a reproach. The word used is not the ordinary term for fear; it names an awe that keeps a person back. Then a reason is given, and it is not wickedness but a failure of comprehension: they are a people who do not grasp things.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, addressed about the group whose promises the previous ayat quoted. The immediate context is a calculation: which side was more dangerous to cross in the Medina of that moment. The commentators read the ayah as diagnosing why the calculation came out as it did, and note that the diagnosis is intellectual rather than moral, which is how the following ayah also ends.

keyTerms.note: A word for fear that holds a person back from acting, distinct from fright. It occurs only here in the Quran, and its root gives the word for a monk, someone whose whole life is organised around it.

The Quran locates thought and feeling in the chest as often as in the heart, and the word carries a sense of what is enclosed and carried about. Saying the dread is in their chests places it where they cannot set it down.

A verb for grasping something from the inside, not merely knowing it. Its negation says the failure is one of penetration rather than of information, which is a gentler and more troubling diagnosis at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Fear was a rational instrument in a society without police. Safety came from being attached to people who would answer for a person, and the practical question in any dispute was who could reach you and how fast. A neighbour with armed cousins was a present danger; a distant authority was not. The ayah takes that entirely sensible arithmetic and points out what it leaves out of the sum.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for restraining dread used here appears only once in the Quran. This ayah and the next both close with the same phrase about a people who do not, yet each ends on a different verb of understanding, one for grasping from within and one for reasoning. These are the only two consecutive ayat where those two exact forms are paired.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Fear is treated as a measuring instrument. What a person dreads most reveals what they actually believe has power, regardless of what they say. That makes the ayah diagnostic rather than accusatory. And the reason given is understanding, not wickedness, which locates the problem where it can still be addressed: someone who has not grasped something can grasp it, whereas someone condemned for malice has nowhere to go.

crossReferences.why: Describes those who deliver God's messages and fear none but Him, the opposite measurement.
Asks whether people are more deserving of fear than God, putting the same comparison as a question.
Ends with the same construction about a people who do not, using the other verb for understanding.

studies.applyIt: Ask yourself which conversation you have been avoiding this month, and who is on the other side of it. Then ask what exactly you are expecting them to do. Usually the answer, said plainly, is smaller than the avoidance suggests. This ayah is about weighing the things we fear against each other honestly.

studies.title: United Only From Outside
studies.meaning: A military observation becomes a description of a condition. They will only fight from behind fortifications, never in the open together, and the reason is supplied at once: their hostility towards one another is severe. Then comes the line that generalises, addressed to the observer. One would reckon them united, and their hearts are scattered. The ayah ends on the same construction as the one before it, with a different verb for understanding.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the description of the groups involved in the episode. The oasis settlements around Medina were separate fortified compounds rather than one town, which made the observation about walls literal. The commentators do not confine the ayah to one group, and they read the closing comment about scattered hearts as the underlying explanation the whole surah has been working towards.

keyTerms.note: The plural of a word for a built wall, occurring only here in the Quran. It is more specific than the general terms for a barrier, naming masonry raised deliberately between people.

A word covering both might and hardship, used for the strength shown in battle and for the distress that comes of it. Saying their force is severe among themselves turns an asset into the thing that divides them.

A plural adjective for things dispersed and unlike one another. It is used elsewhere of the varied plants that come out of one watered ground, so the word carries difference without implying disorder.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: The oasis of Medina was a scatter of fortified compounds, each belonging to a clan, with gardens between them. A group could shut its gate and be effectively out of reach. That architecture shaped politics: alliances formed and dissolved without anyone having to face anyone in the open, and a quarrel could last years while both parties stayed a short walk apart behind their own walls.
studies.didYouKnow: The plural for built walls in this ayah occurs nowhere else in the Quran. The word for scattered appears three times in the whole Book, and one of the others, at 20:53, uses it of the various plants brought out of a single watered soil, so the same adjective covers fruitful variety and a divided heart.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage says that apparent unity and actual unity are different things, and that the difference is measurable by behaviour under pressure. That is not a claim about a single group; it is a general test. Walls make a coalition look like a body. The ayah's closing diagnosis is again a failure of reasoning rather than of will, which keeps the description from hardening into a verdict about persons.

crossReferences.why: Recalls hearts reconciled after enmity as a favour, which is the condition this ayah reports missing.
Says all the wealth on earth could not have united those hearts, but that God united them.
Ends with the same construction about a people who do not, using the other verb for understanding.

studies.applyIt: Think of a group you belong to that looks more united from outside than it feels from inside. Do not try to fix it this week. Just have one honest conversation with one person in it, about something real, without recruiting them to a side. The ayah's diagnosis is scattered hearts. That is what a real conversation works on.

studies.title: The Voice That Walks Away
studies.meaning: Two comparisons stand side by side. The first points to a group shortly before, who tasted the consequence of their own decision; the commentators differ over which group is meant and the Quran does not say. The second is a small scene with dialogue: a voice urges a human being to reject faith, and the moment he does, the same voice separates itself and says it fears God. Nothing intervenes between the urging and the abandonment.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing the surah's account of broken assurances with two comparisons rather than a further argument. The first looks back to a recent reversal the audience would have recognised without being told which one, and the classical sources offer more than one candidate. The second leaves history altogether. Placed here, the pair reframes the whole episode as an instance of an old pattern rather than a local political failure.

keyTerms.note: From a root for a downpour of cold rain and for anything oppressive and hard to digest. The word treats the outcome of a decision as something swallowed, which is why the verb beside it is tasting.
The generic term for a human being with the definite article, not a name and not a group. It turns the scene from an episode into a pattern that any reader can be standing inside.
From a root for being cured and for being quit of a debt. The word describes separation completed rather than denial attempted, which is what makes the desertion in this scene so cold.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabian society ran on guarantors. A man who wanted a loan, a safe passage or a marriage brought someone who would stand behind him, and that person's word was the whole security. There was a formal declaration for withdrawing it, made publicly so that everyone knew the guarantee had lapsed. The scene in these ayat borrows that exact move, and puts it at the worst possible moment.
studies.didYouKnow: The same disowning line appears at 8:48, where it is addressed to a whole army once the two forces come in sight of each other, and the same withdrawal is spoken at 14:22 after judgement is settled. This passage gives the shortest version and the only one aimed at a single person, which is what makes it read less like a report than a warning.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Temptation is portrayed as having no stake in the outcome it produces, which is a specific claim about how evil operates. The urging is loud and the abandonment is instant, with nothing offered in between. The tempter's closing line is the strangest part: it claims fear of God, so even the voice that argued against faith does not dispute the fact of God. What it abandons is the person, not the belief.

crossReferences.why: Gives the same disowning line to a whole army once the two forces come in sight of each other.
Has the same figure explain, after judgement, that he only called and they answered.
States the ending both parties share, which completes the comparison these two ayat set up.

studies.applyIt: Think of the last thing you did that you would not want described plainly, and notice how loud the reasoning was beforehand and how quiet it went afterwards. That gap is the whole subject of these ayat. You do not need to punish yourself over it. Just notice that the voice did not stay.

studies.theme: Time and the Brevity of Life
studies.title: What You Sent For Tomorrow
studies.meaning: The word for tomorrow is doing a lot of work. A whole hereafter is named by the ordinary word for the next day, which shortens the distance to it and makes the accounting immediate. The instruction is to look, and what is to be looked at is what has already been sent ahead, not what is intended. Awareness of God frames the sentence on both sides, repeated before and after, which is unusual even in the Quran.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, at the end of a surah about a broken alliance and an expulsion from Medina. The ayah before closes a short parable in which one party urges another into ruin and then disowns him. That is the immediate background: people who had made promises to each other and did not keep them. The instruction to examine your own account follows directly on a picture of misplaced trust.

keyTerms.note: The plain word for the following day, indefinite here, so it reads as a tomorrow rather than the tomorrow. Classical readers note the effect: the last day is spoken of as near enough to plan for.

A verb of sending something on in advance, used of provisions dispatched before a journey. It makes deeds into baggage that has already left, which is why the ayah asks you to look rather than to decide.
An imperative of seeing, applied to a soul rather than to a person, and phrased in the third person so it lands as a general instruction. The verb is inspection rather than reflection.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan sent goods ahead. A merchant with a long journey dispatched part of his load with an earlier group so it would be waiting at the other end, and the practice had its own vocabulary. What went forward was gone; you could not adjust it once it left. The ayah uses that verb for deeds, addressed to people who had sent consignments ahead and knew the feeling of watching them leave.
studies.didYouKnow: Awareness of God is commanded twice inside this single ayah, once before the instruction and once after it, a doubling the Quran uses sparingly. A few ayat later the surah ends with a run of divine names, one of the densest concentrations anywhere in the Book, so the chapter closes on the one being feared.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Self-examination is put in the imperative and given an object, which distinguishes it from anxiety. You are not told to worry about the outcome; you are told to inspect a record. The choice of the word for tomorrow also does something specific to the doctrine. By using the everyday term rather than a technical one, the passage makes the hereafter continuous with ordinary planning rather than a separate subject a person visits occasionally.

crossReferences.why: Names the opposite of this inspection, forgetting God and losing sight of oneself in the same movement.
Uses the same verb for what was sent forward and adds what was left behind, at the moment of knowing.
Promises that what is sent ahead is found again, which is the encouraging half of the same image.

studies.applyIt: Take five minutes tonight and write down what you actually did today, not what you meant to do. No verdict at the end, no resolutions. The ayah asks for a look at the record, and most people find the surprise is not in what is bad but in how much of the day is unaccounted for.

studies.title: Forgetting God, Losing Yourself
studies.meaning: The consequence named is exact and strange: forgetting God is answered by being made to forget yourself. Nothing is said about punishment yet; the penalty described is a loss of self-knowledge. The classical readers take it as forgetting what benefits you, or forgetting to look after your own soul, and some read it as no longer knowing what you are for. The ayah after refuses the equivalence of two destinations and names one group the winners.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, near the close of a surah occupied with a broken pact and with people who calculated badly. It follows the instruction to look at what you have sent ahead and the parable of one party abandoning another. No specific occasion is reported for these two ayat. They generalise the surah's subject: the surah has been about groups who miscalculated, and here the miscalculation is traced to forgetting.

keyTerms.note: Arabic uses one verb for the memory lapse and for deliberate neglect. The ambiguity is deliberate in the Quran, where forgetting God is rarely an accident and is described as something a person drifts into.
The word means the self and also the soul and the appetite. Being made to forget it can mean losing sight of your own interest or of your own nature, and the commentators keep both.
A participle from a verb for succeeding in a contest and for escaping danger. Both senses run together, so the word carries a prize won and a peril survived at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab memory was professional. There were no archives, so genealogies, treaties, debts and poems were held in the head, and a man known for a bad memory was a man nobody would use as a witness. Forgetting was a public failing rather than a private inconvenience. To be told that you had been made to forget yourself was to be described in the terms a community used for someone no longer reliable.
studies.didYouKnow: A related sentence elsewhere in the Quran says that they forgot God and He forgot them, using the same verb on both sides. Here the second half is changed: what a person loses is not God's attention but their own self. The substitution is the whole point of the ayah, and the classical commentators pause on it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah makes self-knowledge dependent on something outside the self. A person who loses hold of God is described as losing hold of their own account, which reverses the modern order in which you would find yourself first and then decide about God. It also gives the consequence as a description rather than a threat: nothing is inflicted, and the second clause simply reports what follows the first.

crossReferences.why: Runs the same reciprocal structure with a different second half, God's forgetting rather than the self's.
Names another consequence of turning away from remembrance, a narrowed life rather than a lost self.
Gives the positive case, remembrance described as what settles a heart rather than what it costs to lose.

studies.applyIt: Set one fixed point in your day where you say something to God, out loud, for ten seconds. Not a full prayer. The same moment each day, tied to something you already do without fail: the kettle, the car door, the last stair. The ayah describes drift, and the only reliable counter to drift is a fixed point.

studies.title: If A Mountain Had Received It
studies.meaning: A conditional that never happened is used to measure something that did. If this Book had come down on a mountain, the mountain would have gone still and split. The listener is invited to notice what has instead happened: it came down on a human heart, which did not split. Then the ayah names what it has just done, calling it a comparison struck for people, and gives the purpose as thinking rather than trembling.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, three ayat from the end of a surah that has moved from a siege to a parable to self-examination. No specific occasion is reported. The ayah is placed immediately before the surah's closing run of divine names, so it functions as the last thing said about the Book before the last thing said about its Author, and both are addressed to a community that had been hearing revelation for years.

keyTerms.note: The same word used elsewhere of eyes lowered and of the earth lying barren before rain. Applied to a mountain it describes stillness and submission rather than fear as an emotion.

A verb for a crack that opens from within and spreads, used of a vessel giving way. The two participles come in order: first the stillness, then the fracture, which is a sequence rather than a single reaction.

A word for a likeness set beside a thing to make it visible. The ayah labels itself, which is unusual, and then says the purpose is thought, so the image is offered as an instrument rather than as a claim.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mountains were the fixed points of Arabian life. Routes were named by them, tribes claimed them, and a traveller located himself by the shape of a ridge on the horizon rather than by any map. They were the standard of what does not move. Medina itself sat between two lava fields with the bulk of a mountain to the north, a landmark the community used daily for direction.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran elsewhere describes the heavens, the earth and the mountains being offered a trust and refusing it out of fear, with the human being accepting it instead. Read together, the two passages make the same point from opposite ends: the mountain cannot bear what is offered, and a person can, which is presented as both an honour and a risk.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The comparison works by implication rather than by statement. Nothing is said about the reader, and yet the reader is the point: the Book has been landing on human hearts without splitting them, and the ayah leaves the inference to be drawn. That makes it a diagnostic rather than a rebuke. It also assigns the weight to the revelation itself rather than to the response it happens to receive, which keeps the measure independent of anyone's feeling.

crossReferences.why: Shows the mountains declining a burden that a human being accepted, the same contrast from the other direction.
Gives an occasion where a mountain actually did crumble, with Moses collapsing beside it.
Describes the response the comparison is looking for in a person, bodies shivering and then hearts loosening.

studies.applyIt: Read a page of the Quran somewhere you cannot skim: standing up, or out loud, or with a pen, writing down one question you cannot answer. The ayah is about weight arriving without being felt, and the usual reason is speed. Slowing the reading down is the only variable you control.

studies.title: Every Name In One Place
studies.meaning: Three ayat, each beginning with the same two words, and the sequence has a shape. The first names God as the one who knows the hidden and the visible and closes with two names of mercy. The second lists eight names of sovereignty and holiness and ends by declaring Him beyond what is associated with Him. The third turns to making, in three stages: originating, bringing into being, and giving form.
studies.historicalContext: Medinan, closing a surah about an expulsion and a broken alliance. No specific occasion is reported for these ayat. Reports circulate about their recitation morning and evening, and the classical writers treat the passage as a summary placed after the surah's argument rather than as a response to any event. It follows the image of a mountain splitting under the weight of revelation.

keyTerms.note: An intensive form from a root meaning to be free of defect, sharing its letters with the words for purity and for hallowed ground. It states an absence rather than a quality: nothing unworthy attaches.

A rare form used only a few times in the Quran, covering watching over, safeguarding and confirming. It is also used of the Book itself as guardian over earlier scriptures, which links the two senses.
From a root meaning to separate cleanly and to be free of something, the same root behind recovery from illness. It names making as a bringing apart from what was there before.
From the word for a shape or an image. Placed third in the making sequence, it covers the individual features that make one thing distinguishable from another of its kind.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arab names were descriptions. A man was called by what he did or by a feature, and honorific titles were earned in public and used instead of the given name. Tribes recited the titles of a chief when they praised him, and a long list of names was how greatness was expressed in that culture. This passage uses the same form and puts every name in one place.
studies.didYouKnow: These three ayat hold the densest cluster of divine names anywhere in the Quran, and several of the names in the middle ayah occur nowhere else in the Book. The order is not decorative: knowledge first, then sovereignty, then making, so the sequence moves from what God knows to what God rules to what God has produced.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Naming is the whole method here. Nothing is argued and nothing is commanded; the passage works by accumulation, and the effect is a description too large to hold at once. That is deliberate. Placing the names of mercy at the end of the first ayah, before the names of power, also fixes an order: the God who knows everything hidden is introduced as merciful before He is introduced as sovereign.

crossReferences.why: Gives the instruction that this passage supplies material for, calling on God by the names themselves.
Describes God at similar length by denial rather than by naming, the opposite technique for the same purpose.
Compresses into four short lines what this passage expands into a list of names.

studies.applyIt: Pick one name from these three ayat that you would not have chosen, the one that sits least comfortably. Carry it for a week. When something happens, ask what that particular name has to do with it. Most people default to two or three names and never use the rest, which leaves most of the description unopened.
